name: Muscles of the shoulder and upper limb (right)
description: Right shoulder, arm and forearm muscles, with the bones of the upper limb for context.

source.attribution: BodyParts3D, (c) The Database Center for Life Science, licensed under CC Attribution-Share Alike 2.1 Japan
source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Muscles of the upper limb
groups.tip: Three nerves do most of the work: musculocutaneous for the front of the arm, mostly median for the forearm flexors, and radial for everything at the back.

groups.label: Bones (context)
groups.tip: Use your elbow bumps as anchors. Most forearm flexors start at the inner bump, and most extensors at the outer bump.

groups.label: Shoulder and pectoral muscles
groups.tip: SITS names the rotator cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis. The first three grip the greater bump on the arm bone, subscapularis the lesser one.

groups.label: Arm muscles
groups.tip: The front of the arm is BBC: biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis, all run by the musculocutaneous nerve. The triceps at the back uses the radial nerve.

groups.label: Forearm: anterior (flexor) compartment
groups.tip: Lay your other hand on your forearm, thumb outside, and your fingers mark four flexors. Only flexor carpi ulnaris and half of one deep flexor use the ulnar nerve.

groups.label: Forearm: posterior (extensor) compartment
groups.tip: Most start at the outer elbow bump, and all use the radial nerve or its branch. Three thumb muscles frame the snuffbox, the hollow you see when you stretch your thumb back.

content.origin: Limb comes from an old English word for a part of the body.
content.location: This pale frame is your right collarbone, shoulder blade, arm bone, forearm bones and hand. It sits under the muscles as a guide.
content.description: A ghostly pale skeleton that shows where each muscle starts and where it ends.
content.function: The bones are the levers. The muscles pull on them to lift, bend, twist and grip.
content.mnemonic: A muscle usually starts on the steadier bone nearer your body and pulls on the bone it moves. Think of an anchor at the top and a rope to the load.
content.clinical: Muscle pull explains why broken bones shift out of line. After a broken collarbone or arm bone, the muscles tug the pieces apart.
content.hint: Look for the pale frame under everything: collarbone, shoulder blade, arm and forearm bones.

content.origin: From the Greek letter delta, which is a triangle. The muscle looks like an upside-down triangle on your shoulder.
content.location: It forms the round cap of your shoulder. It wraps over the joint from the front, the side and the back.
content.description: A thick triangle with front, middle and back parts. They all meet on the outer side of the arm bone.
content.function: It lifts your arm out to the side, like reaching for a high shelf, once a small cuff muscle starts the move. Its front swings the arm forward and its back swings it behind you.
content.mnemonic: Delta means triangle. Picture a triangle-shaped shoulder pad sitting on top of your arm.
content.clinical: A break near the top of the arm bone or a dislocated shoulder can hurt the axillary nerve that powers it. Lifting the arm sideways gets weak, and a patch of shoulder skin goes numb.
content.hint: The rounded shoulder cap used for vaccine injections, about three finger widths below the bony tip of the shoulder.

questions.text: Which nerve powers the deltoid?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve powers the deltoid. It also supplies teres minor, a small rotator cuff muscle.

questions.text: A break near the top of the arm bone can damage the axillary nerve. Which movement gets weak?
options: Lifting the arm out to the side
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve powers the deltoid, the main muscle that lifts your arm sideways after the first small part of the lift.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a little table. Your left and right traps together make a four-sided shape, a trapezium.
content.location: It spreads over the back of your neck and upper back, from your skull and spine out to the tip of your shoulder.
content.description: A big flat sheet shaped like a kite. It has upper, middle and lower fibres that pull in different directions.
content.function: Its upper part shrugs your shoulders, the middle pulls your shoulder blades back, and the lower part pulls them down. Together they tilt the blade so you can reach overhead.
content.mnemonic: Shrug your shoulders up to your ears. The traps are doing the lifting.
content.clinical: It is powered by the spinal accessory nerve, a cranial nerve. If neck surgery injures this nerve, shrugging gets weak and the shoulder droops.
content.hint: The broad kite-shaped sheet on the upper back that you use to shrug.

questions.text: Which nerve makes the trapezius move?
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve, cranial nerve eleven, drives the trapezius. That is why an injured nerve makes shrugging weak.

content.origin: From the Latin for chest, and major, meaning larger. It is the bigger of your two chest muscles.
content.location: It covers the upper front of your chest. Its lower edge makes the front fold of your armpit, which you can grip between finger and thumb.
content.description: A thick fan with an upper part from the collarbone and a bigger part from the breastbone. Both gather into a flat tendon on the arm bone.
content.function: It pulls your arm across your chest and turns it inward, like giving someone a hug. Its upper part helps lift the arm forward.
content.mnemonic: Pec major gives the hugs. Wrap your arms across your chest and feel it squeeze.
content.clinical: Its tendon can tear off the arm bone during a very heavy bench press. Some people are born missing part of it, a condition called Poland syndrome.
content.hint: The big chest muscle that forms the front wall of your armpit.

questions.text: The front fold of your armpit is formed mainly by which muscle?
questions.explanation: The lower edge of pectoralis major makes the front fold of the armpit. Grip it and you are holding this muscle.

content.origin: From the Latin for chest, and minor, meaning smaller. It hides under its big brother.
content.location: It lies under pectoralis major on the upper front of your chest wall.
content.description: A thin triangle running up and out from ribs three, four and five to a small hook on the shoulder blade called the coracoid.
content.function: It pulls your shoulder blade forward and down, holding it steady against your chest wall.
content.mnemonic: Remember three, four, five to the beak. Coracoid means like a crow's beak, and the muscle runs from ribs three to five up to it.
content.clinical: Surgeons use it as a landmark, because it crosses the main armpit artery and splits it into three parts. When tight, it can press on the nerves to the arm.
content.hint: The smaller chest muscle hidden under the big one, running from the ribs up to a beak-like hook on the shoulder blade.

questions.text: Where on the shoulder blade does pectoralis minor attach?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor runs from ribs three to five up to the coracoid process, the beak-shaped hook on the front of the shoulder blade.

content.origin: From the Latin for saw-toothed, because its edge on the ribs looks like the teeth of a saw.
content.location: It lies on the side of your chest, between the ribs and the shoulder blade. On a lean person you can see its jagged edge below the armpit.
content.description: A wide sheet that grips the top eight ribs with saw-tooth slips, then wraps back round the chest to the shoulder blade.
content.function: It pushes your shoulder blade forward when you punch or push, and tilts it up so you can reach overhead. It keeps the blade pressed flat on your ribs.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the boxer's muscle. It throws your shoulder blade forward with every punch.
content.clinical: Its nerve, the long thoracic nerve, can be injured during armpit surgery. Then the shoulder blade sticks out like a wing when you push against a wall.
content.hint: The saw-toothed muscle on the side of your chest that holds your shoulder blade flat when you push.

questions.text: After armpit surgery, a shoulder blade sticks out like a wing. The nerve to which muscle is likely hurt?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve powers serratus anterior, which holds the shoulder blade against the chest. Without it, the blade lifts off like a wing.

questions.text: What is the main job of serratus anterior on the shoulder blade?
options: Pulling it back toward the spine
Lifting it up toward the ear
Pushing it forward around the chest
questions.explanation: Serratus anterior drives the shoulder blade forward around the chest, as when you throw a punch. This move is called protraction.

content.origin: From the Latin for widest of the back. It is the broadest muscle on your back.
content.location: It covers your middle and lower back and sweeps up to your armpit. With teres major, it forms the back fold of the armpit.
content.description: A huge flat triangle that narrows into a tendon. The tendon twists round to reach the front of the arm bone.
content.function: It pulls your arm down and back and turns it inward, for pull-ups, rowing, climbing and swimming. The thoracodorsal nerve powers it.
content.mnemonic: Call it the swimmer's muscle. It pulls your arm down and back through the water, just like a chin-up.
content.clinical: It is large and has a reliable blood supply. Surgeons often move part of it to rebuild a breast after cancer surgery.
content.hint: The widest muscle of the back, pulling your arm down and back as in a chin-up.

questions.text: Which nerve powers latissimus dorsi?
questions.explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve powers latissimus dorsi. Its name points to the chest and back, where the muscle lives.

questions.text: Which set of arm movements does latissimus dorsi make?
options: Forward, out to the side and turn outward
Back, in to the side and turn inward
Out to the side and turn outward only
Bend the elbow and turn the palm up
questions.explanation: Latissimus dorsi pulls the arm back, draws it in to your side and turns it inward. That is the pull in a chin-up or a swimming stroke.

content.origin: From the Latin for above the spine. It sits above the bony ridge on your shoulder blade.
content.location: It fills the hollow above the ridge on the back of your shoulder blade. Its tendon slips under the bony tip of the shoulder to the top of the arm bone.
content.description: A rotator cuff muscle that packs the upper hollow of the shoulder blade and ends in a tendon over the top of the joint.
content.function: It starts lifting your arm out to the side, for about the first 15 degrees, then the deltoid takes over. It also holds the ball of the arm bone in its socket.
content.mnemonic: The four rotator cuff muscles spell SITS. S for supraspinatus is the starter, sitting on top.
content.clinical: Its tendon is the one most often pinched or torn in the shoulder. It gets squeezed under the bony shoulder tip, so lifting the arm hurts partway up.
content.hint: The cuff muscle in the hollow above the shoulder blade ridge that begins lifting the arm sideways.

questions.text: Which rotator cuff muscle starts lifting your arm out to the side?
questions.explanation: Supraspinatus starts the sideways lift, then the deltoid takes over for the rest.

questions.text: Which rotator cuff tendon is most often pinched under the bony tip of the shoulder?
questions.explanation: The supraspinatus tendon runs right under the shoulder tip, so it is the one most often pinched and torn.

content.origin: From the Latin for below the spine. It sits below the bony ridge on your shoulder blade.
content.location: It fills the big hollow on the back of your shoulder blade, below the bony ridge.
content.description: A thick triangle covering most of the back of the shoulder blade. Its tendon passes behind the shoulder joint.
content.function: It turns your arm outward, like drawing your hand back to throw a ball. It also helps hold the ball of the arm bone in its socket.
content.mnemonic: I in SITS. Infra means under the spine, and it turns the arm out.
content.clinical: It shares the suprascapular nerve with supraspinatus. If that nerve is squeezed, you can see this muscle waste away at the back of the shoulder.
content.hint: The cuff muscle filling the back of the shoulder blade below the ridge, turning the arm outward.

questions.text: Infraspinatus and supraspinatus share which nerve?
questions.explanation: Both get their power from the suprascapular nerve, which runs across the top of the shoulder blade.

content.origin: From the Latin for round, and minor, meaning smaller. It is the smaller of the two round muscles.
content.location: It runs along the outer edge of the back of your shoulder blade, just below infraspinatus.
content.description: A narrow, rounded cuff muscle running up and out to the back of the ball of the arm bone.
content.function: It turns your arm outward and helps hold the ball of the arm bone snug in its socket.
content.mnemonic: T in SITS. Teres minor is in the cuff, teres major is not. Remember: minor is in, major is out.
content.clinical: It shares the axillary nerve with the deltoid. So an injury to that nerve weakens both muscles.
content.hint: The small rounded cuff muscle on the outer edge of the shoulder blade that shares a nerve with the shoulder cap muscle.

questions.text: Which of these is a rotator cuff muscle?
questions.explanation: Teres minor is the T in SITS, the four cuff muscles. Teres major sits just below it but is not part of the cuff.

questions.text: Which nerve powers teres minor?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve powers teres minor, just as it powers the deltoid.

content.origin: From the Latin for under the shoulder blade. It lies on the side of the blade that faces your ribs.
content.location: It covers the front of your shoulder blade, pressed against the ribs. It forms part of the back wall of your armpit.
content.description: The biggest rotator cuff muscle. It fills the front of the shoulder blade, and its tendon crosses the front of the shoulder joint.
content.function: It turns your arm inward, like tucking your hand behind your back. It also holds the ball of the arm bone firmly in its socket.
content.mnemonic: The last S in SITS, on the Side facing the ribs. It alone goes to the lesser bump on the arm bone, while the other three go to the greater bump.
content.clinical: Its tendon guards the front of the shoulder and helps stop it popping out forward. It can tear when the shoulder dislocates forward.
content.hint: The cuff muscle on the front of the shoulder blade, against the ribs, that turns the arm inward.

questions.text: Which rotator cuff muscle attaches to the lesser tubercle, the smaller bump on the arm bone?
questions.explanation: Subscapularis goes to the lesser tubercle at the front. The other three cuff muscles attach to the greater tubercle.

content.origin: From the Latin for round, and major, meaning larger. It is the bigger of the two round muscles.
content.location: It runs from the lower corner of your shoulder blade, below teres minor. With latissimus dorsi it forms the back fold of your armpit.
content.description: A thick, rounded muscle that runs up and out to the front of the arm bone. It is not part of the rotator cuff.
content.function: It pulls your arm in to your side, turns it inward and helps draw it back, like pulling down on a rope.
content.mnemonic: Call it lat's little helper. It does the same jobs as latissimus dorsi, the widest back muscle.
content.clinical: It borders small gaps near the armpit that carry the axillary nerve and blood vessels. Surgeons use it to find them.
content.hint: The thick round muscle from the lower corner of the shoulder blade to the front of the arm bone, helping the widest back muscle.

questions.text: Which muscle is called lat's little helper because it pulls the arm in and turns it inward?
questions.explanation: Teres major shares the jobs of latissimus dorsi, so it earns the nickname lat's little helper.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a diamond shape. Its outline looks like a stretched diamond.
content.location: It lies under the trapezius, between your upper back spine and the inner edge of your shoulder blade.
content.description: A flat, four-sided sheet with fibres running down and out. It sits just below rhomboid minor.
content.function: It squeezes your shoulder blades together, as when you pull back on oars or stand up tall. It also holds the blade against your ribs.
content.mnemonic: The rhomboids row the boat. Pull your shoulder blades back together and you feel them work.
content.clinical: It is a common spot for aching upper back pain in desk workers. If its nerve is injured, the shoulder blade drifts away from the spine.
content.hint: The larger diamond-shaped muscle under the trapezius that squeezes the shoulder blades together.

questions.text: What do the rhomboids do to the shoulder blades?
options: Push them forward around the chest
Pull them back toward the spine
Tilt them up for reaching overhead
questions.explanation: The rhomboids pull the shoulder blades back toward the spine, squeezing them together like rowing.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a diamond shape, and minor, meaning smaller.
content.location: It lies under the trapezius, just above rhomboid major. It runs from the base of your neck to the shoulder blade.
content.description: A narrow band lying above and alongside rhomboid major, like a thin stripe on top.
content.function: It pulls your shoulder blade back toward the spine and holds it snug against your ribs.
content.mnemonic: Minor sits higher. Remember: minor on top, major below.
content.clinical: It shares the dorsal scapular nerve with rhomboid major and levator scapulae. Injury to that nerve weakens all three.
content.hint: The small upper diamond-shaped muscle joining the base of the neck to the shoulder blade, level with its ridge.

questions.text: Compared with rhomboid major, where does rhomboid minor lie?
options: In front of the shoulder blade
questions.explanation: Rhomboid minor starts at the base of the neck and sits just above rhomboid major, which starts lower on the back.

content.origin: From the Latin for lifter of the shoulder blade. Its name tells you its job.
content.location: It runs down the side and back of your neck, under the trapezius, to the upper corner of your shoulder blade.
content.description: A strap-like muscle that twists a little as it runs down from the top of the neck.
content.function: It lifts your shoulder blade, like hitching a heavy bag up on one shoulder. When the blade stays still, it tips your neck to the side.
content.mnemonic: It does what its name says. Levator means lifter, just like an elevator.
content.clinical: It is a common cause of a stiff neck. Tender knots often form near the upper corner of the shoulder blade.
content.hint: The neck muscle that lifts the upper corner of the shoulder blade, starting from the top four neck bones.

questions.text: Where does levator scapulae start?
options: Front of the upper back bones
Upper back spine, T2 to T5
Base of the neck, C7 to T1
Side bumps of the top four neck bones
questions.explanation: Levator scapulae starts on the side bumps of the top four neck vertebrae, then runs down to the shoulder blade.

content.origin: From the Latin for two heads, and brachii, meaning of the arm. It is the two-headed arm muscle.
content.location: It is the muscle on the front of your upper arm, between shoulder and elbow. Make a fist and bend your elbow to see it bulge.
content.description: It has a long head and a short head. The long head's tendon runs through the shoulder joint in a groove on the arm bone.
content.function: It bends your elbow and turns your palm up, like lifting a shopping bag or turning a key. It pulls hardest when your palm faces up.
content.mnemonic: The biceps pulls the cork. It turns the corkscrew with your palm, then bends the elbow to pull the cork out.
content.clinical: The long head tendon can snap, leaving a ball-shaped bulge called a Popeye arm. Tapping its tendon at the elbow tests the C5 and C6 nerves.
content.hint: The two-headed muscle on the front of the arm that turns the palm up and bends the elbow.

questions.text: Besides bending the elbow, what else does biceps brachii do?
options: Lifts the arm to the side
questions.explanation: Biceps is a strong palm-up twister as well as an elbow bender. That is why it helps you turn a screwdriver.

questions.text: Where does the main biceps tendon attach?
options: Radial tuberosity, a bump on the radius
Olecranon, the point of the elbow
Deltoid tuberosity on the arm bone
questions.explanation: The biceps tendon attaches to a bump on the radius. Pulling there lets it twist the forearm as well as bend the elbow.

content.origin: From the Latin for arm. It simply means the muscle of the arm.
content.location: It lies on the front of the lower arm, underneath the biceps, and crosses the front of the elbow.
content.description: A broad, flat muscle covering the lower half of the front of the arm bone.
content.function: It is the main elbow bender, whichever way your palm faces. It works every time you lift a cup or carry a bag.
content.mnemonic: Brachialis is the workhorse. It pulls on the ulna, which cannot twist, so it bends the elbow in any hand position.
content.clinical: After a bad elbow injury, bleeding into this muscle can turn into bone. This stiffens the elbow and is called myositis ossificans.
content.hint: The deep workhorse elbow bender under the two-headed arm muscle, attaching to the ulna.

questions.text: Which muscle bends the elbow equally well with the palm up or down, because it pulls on the ulna?
questions.explanation: Brachialis attaches to the ulna, which does not twist. So it bends the elbow in every hand position.

content.origin: Named from the coracoid, the crow's beak on the shoulder blade, plus brachium, meaning arm. It runs from the beak to the arm.
content.location: It lies high on the inner side of your upper arm, beside and under the short head of the biceps.
content.description: A slender muscle with a nerve passing right through it.
content.function: It lifts your arm forward and draws it in to your side, like clamping a newspaper under your arm.
content.mnemonic: Its name is its map. Coraco means the coracoid and brachialis means the arm, so it runs from one to the other.
content.clinical: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it, and the main arm artery runs along its inner side. Surgeons use it to find both.
content.hint: The slender upper-arm muscle from the shoulder blade's beak to the arm bone, with its own nerve passing through it.

questions.text: Which nerve passes right through coracobrachialis?
questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, then goes on to power the muscles on the front of the arm.

content.origin: From the Latin for three heads. It is the three-headed muscle of the arm.
content.location: It fills the whole back of your upper arm. Push up from a chair and you can feel it firm up.
content.description: Three heads, called long, lateral and medial, join into one tendon at the point of your elbow.
content.function: It straightens your elbow, as in a push-up or pushing a door open. The radial nerve powers all three heads.
content.mnemonic: Tri means three heads, and triceps straightens. Biceps bends, triceps straightens.
content.clinical: Tapping its tendon tests the C7 nerve. A break in the middle of the arm bone can hurt the radial nerve, which runs in a groove between its heads.
content.hint: The three-headed muscle on the back of the arm that straightens the elbow.

questions.text: Which nerve powers triceps brachii?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve powers all three heads of triceps. It winds round the back of the arm bone right beside them.

questions.text: Where does triceps brachii attach at the elbow?
options: Olecranon, the point of the elbow
questions.explanation: Triceps pulls on the olecranon, the bony point of your elbow. That pull straightens your arm.

content.origin: From the Greek word for elbow. It is simply the elbow muscle.
content.location: A small muscle on the back of your elbow, on the outer side, just below the triceps tendon.
content.description: A small triangle that partly blends with the triceps above it.
content.function: It helps triceps straighten your elbow and keeps the elbow joint steady as you move.
content.mnemonic: Ankon means elbow. Think of it as the little elbow helper.
content.clinical: Surgeons use it as a guide when they open the outer side of the elbow to reach the top of the radius.
content.hint: The small triangle at the back of the elbow, running from the outer bump of the arm bone to the ulna.

questions.text: Anconeus helps which muscle?
questions.explanation: Anconeus helps triceps straighten the elbow. It sits right below the triceps tendon.

content.origin: From the Latin for turning face down, and teres, meaning round.
content.location: It slants across the upper front of your forearm, from the inner elbow to the middle of the radius. It forms the inner edge of the elbow pit.
content.description: A round muscle with two heads. The median nerve passes between them.
content.function: It turns your palm down, like flipping your hand over to type or use a mouse. It also helps bend the elbow.
content.mnemonic: Lay your other hand across the front of this forearm, thumb near the elbow. Your thumb covers pronator teres, the first of four surface muscles.
content.clinical: The median nerve can get squeezed between its two heads. This causes forearm ache and tingling on the thumb side of the hand, called pronator syndrome.
content.hint: The round, slanting muscle that turns the palm down and forms the inner edge of the elbow pit.

questions.text: Which muscle forms the inner edge of the elbow pit, the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: Pronator teres makes the inner edge of the elbow pit, and brachioradialis makes the outer edge.

questions.text: In pronator syndrome, which nerve gets squeezed between the two heads of pronator teres?
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres, so a tight muscle can squeeze it.

content.origin: From the Latin for bender of the wrist on the radius side. The radius is on your thumb side.
content.location: It lies on the surface of the front of the forearm, beside pronator teres. At the wrist, feel its tendon just on the thumb side of the middle tendon.
content.description: A surface wrist bender with a long tendon that slides through its own groove in a small wrist bone.
content.function: It bends your wrist forward and tips your hand toward the thumb side.
content.mnemonic: Lay your hand across your forearm, thumb near the elbow. Your index finger covers flexor carpi radialis.
content.clinical: It is a handy landmark. You feel the radial pulse at the wrist just to the thumb side of its tendon.
content.hint: The surface wrist bender on the thumb side, with the wrist pulse just beside its tendon.

questions.text: You feel the radial pulse just on the thumb side of which tendon?
questions.explanation: The radial artery runs just beside the flexor carpi radialis tendon at the wrist. Press gently there to feel your pulse.

content.origin: From the Latin for palm, and longus, meaning long. It has a long tendon to your palm.
content.location: It lies on the surface of the front of the forearm, between the two wrist benders. Its tendon runs down the middle of your wrist.
content.description: A small muscle belly with a very long thin tendon, like a balloon on a string.
content.function: It helps bend your wrist and tightens the tough sheet in your palm, which helps you cup and grip.
content.mnemonic: Your middle finger covers it in the hand-on-forearm trick. Touch thumb to little finger and bend your wrist to make its tendon pop up.
content.clinical: About one in seven people do not have it at all. Surgeons often borrow its tendon as a graft, and the median nerve lies right under it at the wrist.
content.hint: The thin middle wrist tendon that pops up when you pinch thumb to little finger, though not everyone has one.

questions.text: Which forearm muscle is missing in some people and often used as a tendon graft?
questions.explanation: Palmaris longus is missing in about one in seven people. Its spare tendon is a favourite for grafts.

content.origin: From the Latin for bender of the wrist on the ulna side. The ulna is on your little-finger side.
content.location: It runs down the front of the forearm along the little-finger side. It is the innermost of the surface muscles.
content.description: A two-headed wrist bender. Its tendon holds a pea-shaped bone, the pisiform, that you can feel at the wrist.
content.function: It bends your wrist and tips your hand toward the little finger, like swinging a hammer down onto a nail.
content.mnemonic: Your ring finger covers it in the hand-on-forearm trick. It is the one surface flexor run by the ulnar nerve.
content.clinical: The ulnar nerve, your funny bone nerve, slips between its two heads. Squeezing here, in the cubital tunnel, causes tingling in the little finger.
content.hint: The little-finger-side wrist bender that ends at the pea-shaped wrist bone and is run by the funny bone nerve.

questions.text: Which surface forearm flexor is powered by the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve?
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris runs on the ulnar nerve. The other surface flexors all use the median nerve.

content.origin: From the Latin for bender of the fingers, near the surface. It is the shallower of the two long finger benders.
content.location: It sits in the middle layer of the front of the forearm, under the wrist benders and on top of the deep finger bender.
content.description: A broad muscle with four tendons that pass through the carpal tunnel. Each tendon splits in two to let a deeper tendon pass through.
content.function: It bends the middle joint of each finger, like curling your fingers round a bag handle. It also helps bend the knuckles and wrist.
content.mnemonic: Superficialis splits in two to let profundus through. The surface one stops at the middle bone, the deep one goes to the tip.
content.clinical: To test it, hold the other fingers straight and bend one finger at its middle joint. Cuts across the palm often sever these tendons.
content.hint: The middle-layer finger bender whose split tendons reach the middle finger bones.

questions.text: Where do the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis attach?
questions.explanation: Each tendon splits and attaches to the sides of the middle finger bone. That is why it bends the middle joint.

content.origin: From the Latin for bender of the fingers, deep. It lies deeper than the other finger bender.
content.location: It lies in the deepest layer of the front of the forearm, on the ulna, under flexor digitorum superficialis.
content.description: A large deep muscle with four tendons. They pass through the carpal tunnel and through the split surface tendons to the fingertips.
content.function: It is the only muscle that bends your fingertips, like curling them to scratch an itch. The ulnar nerve runs its little-finger side and a median nerve branch its index side.
content.mnemonic: Profundus is deep and goes to the tips. The deep muscle reaches the very end of each finger.
content.clinical: Its tendon can rip off the fingertip when you grab a jersey, often on the ring finger. Afterwards that fingertip cannot bend.
content.hint: The deep finger bender with two nerves, the only muscle that bends the fingertips.

questions.text: Which is the only muscle that bends the fingertip joints?
questions.explanation: Only flexor digitorum profundus reaches the fingertip bones, so only it can bend the last joint.

questions.text: The part of flexor digitorum profundus going to the ring and little fingers is powered by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve runs the ring and little finger part. A branch of the median nerve runs the index and middle part.

content.origin: From the Latin for long bender of the thumb.
content.location: It lies in the deep layer of the front of the forearm, on the radius, beside the deep finger bender.
content.description: A deep muscle with a single tendon that runs through the carpal tunnel to the tip of the thumb.
content.function: It bends the tip of your thumb, which you need to pinch, hold a pen or turn a key. It also helps bend the thumb's other joints.
content.mnemonic: The long flexor of the thumb goes the whole long way, from forearm to thumb tip.
content.clinical: Its nerve, a median nerve branch called the anterior interosseous nerve, also runs the index part of the deep finger bender. If injured, you cannot make a round OK sign.
content.hint: The deep forearm muscle on the radius that bends the tip of the thumb.

questions.text: Someone cannot make a round OK sign with thumb and index tips. The nerve to which muscle is hurt?
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve powers flexor pollicis longus and the index part of the deep finger bender. Without it, the OK circle flattens into a pinch.

content.origin: From the Latin for turning face down, and quadratus, meaning square.
content.location: It is the deepest muscle just above the front of your wrist, lying right on the radius and ulna.
content.description: A flat, square muscle stretched across between the lower ends of the two forearm bones.
content.function: It is the main muscle that turns your palm down, like flipping your hand over on a table. It also holds the two forearm bones together.
content.mnemonic: Quadratus means square. It is the square palm-down muscle at the bottom of the forearm.
content.clinical: It lies right over a common spot for a broken wrist. Surgeons lift it aside to fix the radius with a metal plate.
content.hint: The small square muscle deep in the lower forearm that turns the palm down.

questions.text: Where is pronator quadratus found?
options: Deep in the front of the forearm, near the wrist
On the front of the arm bone
questions.explanation: Pronator quadratus is the deepest muscle at the front of the lower forearm, just above the wrist.

content.origin: From the Latin for arm, plus radius. It runs from the arm bone down to the radius.
content.location: It is the fleshy muscle on the thumb side of your forearm, just below the elbow. It forms the outer edge of the elbow pit.
content.description: A long surface muscle with a flat tendon to the lower radius. It sits with the back forearm muscles and is powered by the radial nerve.
content.function: It bends your elbow, strongest with your thumb pointing up, like lifting a hammer or a mug.
content.mnemonic: Call it the mug-lifting muscle. It lifts your drink with your thumb pointing up.
content.clinical: Tapping its tendon near the thumb side of the wrist tests the C5 and C6 nerves. This is the brachioradialis reflex.
content.hint: The surface muscle on the thumb side of the forearm that bends the elbow with the thumb pointing up.

questions.text: Brachioradialis bends the elbow, but which nerve powers it?
questions.explanation: Although it bends the elbow, brachioradialis sits with the back forearm muscles and is powered by the radial nerve.

content.origin: From the Latin for long straightener of the wrist on the radius side.
content.location: It lies on the thumb side of the back of the forearm, just behind brachioradialis.
content.description: A long wrist straightener whose tendon runs down the back of the radius, beside its shorter partner, to the index finger's hand bone.
content.function: It pulls your wrist back and tips it toward the thumb. It holds the wrist steady so you can make a firm fist.
content.mnemonic: The two radial extensors go to hand bones two and three. Remember: longus to two, brevis to three.
content.clinical: Your grip is weak unless these muscles hold the wrist back. Radial nerve damage causes wrist drop, where the hand flops down.
content.hint: The long wrist straightener beside the thumb-side elbow bender, going to the index finger's hand bone.

questions.text: Extensor carpi radialis longus attaches to the base of which hand bone?
questions.explanation: The long radial extensor goes to the second metacarpal, the index finger's hand bone. The short one goes to the third.

content.origin: From the Latin for short straightener of the wrist on the radius side.
content.location: It lies on the back of the forearm, just under and inside its longer partner.
content.description: A shorter wrist straightener starting from the outer bump of the elbow. Its tendon runs beside the long one to the middle finger's hand bone.
content.function: It pulls your wrist back and steadies it, like when you hold a racket or lift a kettle.
content.mnemonic: Brevis goes to the middle. It ends on the third hand bone, right in the centre of the wrist.
content.clinical: Tennis elbow usually starts where this muscle attaches to the outer elbow bump. Gripping and lifting then hurt.
content.hint: The short radial wrist straightener from the outer elbow bump, the usual spot for tennis elbow.

questions.text: Tennis elbow most often affects where which muscle starts?
questions.explanation: Tennis elbow is overuse at the outer elbow bump, and extensor carpi radialis brevis is the muscle most often involved.

content.origin: From the Latin for straightener of the fingers.
content.location: It runs down the middle of the back of your forearm, right under the skin.
content.description: A surface muscle that splits into four tendons. They fan across the back of your hand, linked by small bands.
content.function: It straightens your four fingers, like opening your hand to let go of a ball. It is powered by the posterior interosseous nerve, a radial nerve branch.
content.mnemonic: The common finger straightener: one muscle, four tendons, four fingers.
content.clinical: You can see its tendons on the back of your hand when you straighten your fingers. They can be cut in hand injuries or snap in rheumatoid arthritis.
content.hint: The middle surface muscle on the back of the forearm whose four tendons straighten the fingers.

questions.text: Which nerve powers extensor digitorum?
questions.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve, a deep branch of the radial nerve, powers extensor digitorum.

content.origin: From the Latin for straightener of the smallest finger.
content.location: It lies on the surface of the back of the forearm, between the main finger straightener and the ulnar wrist straightener.
content.description: A slender muscle, often partly joined to the main finger straightener, with a tendon to the little finger.
content.function: It straightens your little finger on its own, like lifting your pinkie while holding a cup.
content.mnemonic: Minimi means smallest. It straightens the smallest finger.
content.clinical: With extensor indicis, it lets you raise your index and little fingers on their own, as in the rock and roll horns sign.
content.hint: The slender extra straightener that lets the smallest finger lift on its own.

questions.text: Which finger does extensor digiti minimi straighten?
questions.explanation: Digiti minimi means of the smallest finger, so it straightens your little finger.

content.origin: From the Latin for straightener of the wrist on the ulna side.
content.location: It is the innermost surface muscle on the back of the forearm, running along the back of the ulna.
content.description: A long surface muscle whose tendon runs in a groove beside the knobbly end of the ulna, then on to the little finger's hand bone.
content.function: It pulls your wrist back and tips it toward the little finger, like wiping a table from side to side.
content.mnemonic: It teams up with flexor carpi ulnaris. The two ulnar muscles pull your hand toward the ulna.
content.clinical: Its tendon can slip out of its groove in sports that twist the wrist, like tennis and golf.
content.hint: The little-finger-side wrist straightener running along the back of the ulna to the fifth hand bone.

questions.text: Which pair of muscles together tip the hand toward the little finger?
options: Flexor carpi radialis and extensor carpi radialis longus
Palmaris longus and extensor carpi radialis brevis
Flexor digitorum superficialis and extensor digitorum
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris both pull the hand toward the ulna, on the little-finger side.

content.origin: From the Latin for turning face up, like lying on your back.
content.location: It lies deep in the upper back and outer side of your forearm, wrapped round the top of the radius.
content.description: A sheet-like deep muscle that curls round the radius like a sling. A branch of the radial nerve passes through it.
content.function: It turns your palm up, like holding out your hand for a coin. It does this best when your elbow is straight.
content.mnemonic: It does what it says. The supinator supinates, with the biceps as its powerful partner.
content.clinical: The deep branch of the radial nerve can be squeezed where it enters this muscle. Then straightening the fingers and thumb gets weak.
content.hint: The deep muscle wrapped round the top of the radius that turns the palm up, with a nerve branch passing through it.

questions.text: Supinator works with which muscle to turn the palm up?
questions.explanation: Biceps brachii is the powerful partner of supinator. Supinator does the light work and biceps adds force, like twisting a stiff lid.

content.origin: From the Latin for long muscle that moves the thumb away.
content.location: It lies in the deep layer of the back of the forearm. Its tendon curls round the thumb side of the wrist to the thumb.
content.description: A deep muscle whose tendon, with its short partner, forms the front edge of the anatomical snuffbox, the hollow at the base of your thumb.
content.function: It moves your thumb away from your palm, like opening your hand to grab a big jar. It also helps straighten the thumb and tip the wrist.
content.mnemonic: The long abductor and the short extensor travel together. Think of them as two thumb tendons sharing one tunnel.
content.clinical: When the shared tunnel of these two tendons gets inflamed, it is called De Quervain tenosynovitis. Moving the thumb and wrist then hurts, and the Finkelstein test is positive.
content.hint: The deep thumb muscle that swings the thumb away from the palm and edges the snuffbox with its short partner.

questions.text: De Quervain tenosynovitis affects abductor pollicis longus and which other tendon?
questions.explanation: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis share a tunnel at the wrist. When it swells, both tendons hurt.

content.origin: From the Latin for short straightener of the thumb.
content.location: It lies deep in the back of the forearm, just below the long thumb abductor. Its tendon runs beside it to the thumb.
content.description: A short deep muscle whose tendon forms part of the front edge of the anatomical snuffbox.
content.function: It straightens your thumb at its base knuckle, like sticking your thumb out to hitch a ride.
content.mnemonic: Brevis is short, so it stops short at the first thumb bone. Longus goes all the way to the tip.
content.clinical: It gets inflamed with the long thumb abductor in De Quervain tenosynovitis, causing pain on the thumb side of the wrist.
content.hint: The short thumb straightener that stops at the first thumb bone and travels with the long thumb abductor.

questions.text: Where does extensor pollicis brevis attach?
options: Base of the thumb tip bone
Base of the first thumb bone
Base of the thumb hand bone
questions.explanation: Brevis means short, so it stops at the first bone of the thumb, the proximal phalanx.

content.origin: From the Latin for long straightener of the thumb.
content.location: It lies deep in the back of the forearm. Its tendon hooks round a bump on the back of the radius and forms the back edge of the snuffbox.
content.description: A deep muscle with a long tendon that turns round a small bump on the radius, called Lister's tubercle, like a rope round a pulley.
content.function: It straightens every joint of your thumb, right to the tip, like flicking your thumb up and back.
content.mnemonic: Longus goes the long way, round Lister's tubercle and on to the thumb tip.
content.clinical: Weeks after a broken wrist, its tendon can wear through where it rubs on the bump. Then you cannot lift the tip of your thumb.
content.hint: The long thumb straightener that hooks round the bump on the back of the radius and forms the back edge of the snuffbox.

questions.text: Which tendon forms the back edge of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: Extensor pollicis longus forms the back edge. The long abductor and short extensor form the front edge.

content.origin: From the Latin for straightener of the index finger, your pointing finger.
content.location: It is the lowest muscle in the deep layer of the back of the forearm, on the lower ulna.
content.description: A narrow deep muscle whose tendon joins the main index finger tendon on its inner side.
content.function: It straightens your index finger on its own so you can point. It also helps pull the wrist back.
content.mnemonic: Indicis means index. It is your pointing muscle.
content.clinical: Surgeons often move its tendon to replace a snapped long thumb straightener, extensor pollicis longus.
content.hint: The deep muscle on the lower ulna that lets you point with your index finger on its own.

questions.text: Which muscle lets your index finger straighten on its own?
questions.explanation: Extensor indicis gives the index finger its own straightener, so you can point while the other fingers stay curled.
